Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 12 periods = 540 minutes
Total: 12 periods · 9h 0min

periods.activity_title: What Makes a Rectangle? Diagonals Tell the Story

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find all other angles inside the rectangle with one marked angle of 30° (at vertex A).
Find all other angles inside the rectangle with one marked angle of 110° (at vertex P).
Consider a circle with centre O. Line segments PL and AM are two perpendicular diameters. Reason and/or experiment to determine what figure APML is.

homework.description: Without paper (only two equal-length sticks and a thread), construct an exact 90° angle. Explain the method.

time_bands.activity: Pose the Carpenter's Problem: two equal wooden strips are to be joined so their endpoints form a rectangle. Ask students what condition on the strips would guarantee a rectangle, collecting intuitions before any definition is given.

Introduce the five properties of a rectangle (all angles 90°; opposite sides equal and parallel; diagonals equal and bisecting) and trace Deductions 1–2: diagonals of a rectangle are equal (SAS congruence) and bisect each other (AAS congruence). Students record the congruence arguments in their own words.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1(i), p.94 ("Find all other angles inside the rectangle with one marked angle of 30°....") and Figure it Out Q1(ii), p.94 ("Find all other angles inside the rectangle with one marked angle of 110°...."), applying the 90° angle property and diagonal relationships. Pairs compare answers and reconcile differences.

Class investigates Figure it Out Q3, p.94 ("Consider a circle with centre O. Line segments PL and AM are two perpendicular diameters...."), reasoning from the equal-bisecting-diagonal property to identify the quadrilateral formed.

periods.teacher_notes: Students commonly assume that 'opposite sides equal' alone defines a rectangle; Deduction 4's result — that all angles being 90° is sufficient — directly challenges this, and is worth flagging before the class moves to the exercises. For a self-study extension, Figure it Out Q4, p.94 ("Without paper (only two equal-length sticks and a thread), construct an exact 90° angle....") is set as homework and offers a neat application of the equal-bisecting-diagonal principle.

periods.activity_title: Squares as Special Rectangles: Deducing Diagonal Properties

textbook_items_in_class.description: Can the three equalities (AO = CO, ∠AOB = ∠COD as vertically opposite angles, and AD = CB) be used to establish ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB? Examine whether these three conditions are sufficient for a congruence condition.
Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm, bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of 30°.
Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm, bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of 90°.
Can 'opposite sides parallel and equal' serve as a definition of a rectangle? That is, is every such quadrilateral a rectangle? (Try This prompt)

homework.description: Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm, bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of 40°.
Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm, bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of 140°.

time_bands.activity: Revisit Deduction 3: starting from equal, mutually bisecting diagonals crossing at angle x, students derive all four interior angles algebraically and confirm they are all 90°, establishing that the crossing angle does not determine the shape — the bisecting and equal conditions do.

Introduce squares as the subclass of rectangles in which all sides are equal, display the Venn diagram placing squares within rectangles. Work through Deduction 5 (SSS congruence forcing diagonal perpendicularity in a square) and list the five properties of squares.

Discuss Math Talk, p.84 ("Can the three equalities AO = CO, ∠AOB = ∠COD as vertically opposite angles, and AD = CB be used to establish ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB?..."), asking students to identify which congruence condition applies and whether the given set is sufficient. Then tackle Math Talk Q5, p.94 ("Can 'opposite sides parallel and equal' serve as a definition of a rectangle?...") as a whole-class deductive argument.

Students construct the quadrilaterals in Figure it Out Q2(i), p.94 ("Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm, bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of 30°....") and Figure it Out Q2(iii), p.94 ("Draw a quadrilateral whose diagonals have equal lengths of 8 cm, bisect each other, and intersect at an angle of 90°...."), compare the two resulting shapes, and reason about why one is a rectangle and the other a square.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error here is assuming that equal and bisecting diagonals are sufficient for a square — Deduction 5 clarifies that perpendicularity is the additional condition needed, and the contrast between the 30° and 90° crossing constructions makes this tangible. Watch for students who attempt to verify the Math Talk congruence claim by measurement rather than identifying the correct congruence condition.

periods.activity_title: Why Four Angles Must Sum to 360°: A Diagonal Argument

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 40° (at vertex R).

time_bands.activity: Pose the opening question from section 4.2: can a quadrilateral have three right angles and a fourth that is not 90°? Students draw several quadrilaterals of their own, measure all four angles, and record the sums. The pattern that the sum is always near 360° is noted without yet being explained.

Students draw a diagonal in one of their quadrilaterals, labelling the six resulting triangle angles. They identify which pairs of triangle angles together form each quadrilateral angle, count the total, and arrive at 360° as the sum of two triangles' 180° each. The class then formalises this as the angle-sum theorem, applicable to any quadrilateral.

Return to the opening question: use the angle-sum theorem to show that three right angles (270°) leave exactly 90° for the fourth — making a rectangle the only possibility. Students write a one-sentence justification in their own words.

Bridge to parallelograms: students tackle Figure it Out Q1(i), p.102 ("Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 40° at vertex R....") as a first application of angle reasoning in a shape with parallel sides, anticipating the co-interior angle result.

periods.teacher_notes: The key reasoning step — that the diagonal's six angles partition exactly into the four quadrilateral angles — is one students often accept numerically without seeing structurally; ask pairs to point to each quadrilateral angle and name which triangle angles make it up. Figure it Out Q1(i), p.102 is drawn from section 4.3 and serves here as a natural bridge; it will be revisited when section 4.3 is formally treated.

textbook_segments.title: More Quadrilaterals with Parallel Opposite Sides

periods.activity_title: Parallelograms: Proving Angles, Sides, and Diagonals

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 40° (at vertex R).
Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 110° (at vertex E).
Find the remaining angles in the rhombus with one marked angle of 30° (at vertex U).
Find the remaining angles in the quadrilateral with a marked angle of 20° (at vertex A).

time_bands.activity: Construct a parallelogram by drawing two non-perpendicular pairs of parallel lines and label it. Define a parallelogram as a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel, then display the Venn diagram placing rectangles as a special subclass.

Walk through Deductions 6, 7, and 8: using a general angle x, derive that adjacent angles sum to 180° and opposite angles are equal (co-interior angles, Deduction 6); prove opposite sides equal by AAS congruence on the diagonal triangles (Deduction 7); prove diagonals bisect each other by ASA congruence using alternate angles (Deduction 8). Students record each deduction with its congruence condition.

Students apply the four properties of parallelograms to Figure it Out Q1(i), p.102 ("Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 40°....") and Figure it Out Q1(ii), p.102 ("Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 110°...."), then extend to Figure it Out Q1(iii), p.102 ("Find the remaining angles in the rhombus with one marked angle of 30°....") as a preview of rhombus properties.
Students work on Figure it Out Q1(iv), p.102 ("Find the remaining angles in the quadrilateral with a marked angle of 20°....") individually, then a volunteer explains the angle-chain reasoning aloud.

periods.teacher_notes: A frequent error is applying the supplementary-angles rule to opposite angles instead of adjacent ones; reinforce that co-interior angles arise on the same side of the transversal. The progression from Deduction 6 to Deduction 8 mirrors the logical build-up from angle to side to diagonal, which helps students see the properties as connected rather than isolated facts.

textbook_segments.title: More Quadrilaterals with Parallel Opposite Sides

periods.activity_title: Constructing Parallelograms and Rhombuses from Diagonal Data

textbook_items_in_class.description: Using diagonal properties, construct a parallelogram whose diagonals are of lengths 7 cm and 5 cm and intersect at an angle of 140°.
Using diagonal properties, construct a rhombus whose diagonals are of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm.

time_bands.activity: Review the diagonal-bisection properties established for parallelograms (Deduction 8) and note that they are the key tool for construction: bisecting diagonals mean each half-diagonal is known, so a compass-and-ruler construction is possible.

Students construct the parallelogram in Figure it Out Q2, p.102 ("Using diagonal properties, construct a parallelogram whose diagonals are of lengths 7 cm and 5 cm and intersect at an angle of 140°...."), working step-by-step: mark the intersection point, lay off half-diagonals at 140° and 40°, connect the four endpoints. Pairs check each other's figures.

Students construct the rhombus in Figure it Out Q3, p.102 ("Using diagonal properties, construct a rhombus whose diagonals are of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm...."), using the perpendicular-bisector property of rhombus diagonals. They verify the four sides are equal by measurement.
Class discusses: what changes in the construction process when moving from a general parallelogram to a rhombus? Students articulate the additional perpendicularity constraint in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who halve only one diagonal when constructing — both diagonals must be bisected at the intersection point. The contrast between the 140° crossing of the parallelogram and the 90° crossing of the rhombus reinforces that perpendicular diagonals are a special, not universal, parallelogram property.

periods.activity_title: Rhombuses: All Sides Equal, All Parallelogram Properties Follow

textbook_items_in_class.description: Using diagonal properties, construct a rhombus whose diagonals are of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm.

time_bands.activity: Construct a rhombus by fixing two equal adjacent sides at an arbitrary angle and locating the fourth vertex via equal-radius arcs, showing the figure exists for any non-straight angle. Students measure all four sides to confirm equality.

Work through Deduction 9: the diagonal of a rhombus creates two isosceles triangles; base angles are equal; use this to show opposite angles equal and adjacent angles supplementary; then use the equal diagonal angles as alternate angles to prove opposite sides parallel — establishing that every rhombus is a parallelogram. List the six properties of a rhombus.

Work through Deduction 10: at the intersection of the two diagonals, SSS congruence of the two half-triangles forces the two angles to be equal and supplementary, so each is 90°. Students write the argument step by step in their notebooks.

Revisit Figure it Out Q3, p.102 ("Using diagonal properties, construct a rhombus whose diagonals are of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm....") with the perpendicularity proof now in hand, and verify that the constructed figure's diagonal crossing angle is indeed 90°.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes conflate 'all sides equal' with 'all angles equal'; the explicit algebraic angle-derivation in Deduction 9 — showing adjacent angles are supplementary but not necessarily equal — is worth pausing on. Deduction 10's SSS argument is structurally identical to Deduction 5 for squares, so drawing that parallel helps students see the logical family tree.

periods.activity_title: Geoboard Diagonals and Triangle Joins: Quadrilaterals from Construction

textbook_items_in_class.description: Geoboard Activity: place two rubber bands as perpendicular equal-length diagonals, join the ends to form a quadrilateral, identify and justify its type; then extend one diagonal by 2 cm on both sides and re-identify the resulting quadrilateral.

Joining Triangles Activity: (1) join two equilateral triangle cutouts (8 cm sides) along a common edge and identify the quadrilateral; (2) join two isosceles triangle cutouts (8, 8, 6 cm) in two different orientations and identify each resulting quadrilateral; (3) join two scalene triangle cutouts (6, 9, 12 cm) in different ways and identify the resulting quadrilaterals. Justify each answer.

time_bands.activity: Students cut out the required triangle shapes: two equilateral (8 cm), two isosceles (8, 8, 6 cm), and two scalene (6, 9, 12 cm) from plain card. Each group also prepares a geoboard or dot-paper substitute.

Groups carry out Activity 1 (Geoboard), p.103 ("place two rubber bands as perpendicular equal-length diagonals, join the ends to form a quadrilateral, identify and justify its type; then extend one diagonal by 2 cm on both sides...."), recording both quadrilateral identifications and their diagonal-property justifications.

Groups carry out Activity 2 (Joining Triangles), p.103–105 ("join two equilateral triangle cutouts along a common edge and identify the quadrilateral; join two isosceles triangle cutouts in two different orientations...."), working through all three triangle-pair cases. For each resulting shape they name the quadrilateral and write a one-sentence justification.

Groups share findings: each group presents one case from the triangle-joining activity, stating the quadrilateral produced and the diagonal or side property that justifies the identification. Class resolves any disagreements collectively.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may not immediately see that joining two equilateral triangles along a common edge yields a rhombus — prompt them to check whether all four sides are equal before identifying the shape. For the isosceles triangle pair, the two different orientations (joined at the base versus at a lateral edge) should produce different quadrilaterals; if a group gets the same shape both ways, ask them to recheck the joining edge.

periods.activity_title: Defining Kites and Trapeziums: Properties from Definitions

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find all the sides and the angles of the quadrilateral obtained by joining two equilateral triangles with sides 4 cm.
Construct a kite whose diagonals are of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm.
Find the remaining angles in the trapezium with one marked angle of 100°.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the kite: a quadrilateral ABCD with AB = BC and CD = DA (two pairs of consecutive equal sides). Students draw several kites freehand, label the equal-side pairs, and note which diagonal connects the vertices between unequal sides versus the vertices between equal sides.

Introduce the trapezium as a quadrilateral with at least one pair of parallel opposite sides. Students construct a trapezium using a set square, then use co-interior angle properties (∠S + ∠P = 180° and ∠R + ∠Q = 180° for PQ ∥ SR) to find the remaining angles from one given angle. Work through Figure it Out Q3(i), p.107 ("Find the remaining angles in the trapezium with one marked angle of 100°....").

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, p.107 ("Find all the sides and the angles of the quadrilateral obtained by joining two equilateral triangles with sides 4 cm...."), linking back to the equilateral-triangle join from the previous activity and now formally computing the angles of the resulting rhombus using its properties.

Students begin constructing the kite in Figure it Out Q2, p.107 ("Construct a kite whose diagonals are of lengths 6 cm and 8 cm...."), noting that the diagonals of a kite are perpendicular and that one bisects the other.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse which diagonal of a kite is the axis of symmetry; reinforce that the diagonal connecting the vertices between equal-side pairs (BD in ABCD) is the one that bisects the other diagonal at right angles and bisects the vertex angles. The construction in Figure it Out Q2, p.107 makes this visible through compass work rather than memorisation.

periods.activity_title: Proving Kite Symmetry and Isosceles Trapezium Base Angles

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the remaining angles in the trapezium with one marked angle of 105°.
Find the remaining angles in the trapezium with one marked angle of 135°.
PAIR and RODS are two rectangles sharing vertex R with OR = 5 cm and ∠P = 30°. Find ∠IOD.
What type of quadrilateral has opposite sides equal? Justify your answer. (Hint: draw a diagonal and check for congruent triangles.)

time_bands.activity: Prove Property 1 of the kite: diagonal BD bisects both vertex angles ∠ABC and ∠ADC, and is the perpendicular bisector of diagonal AC. Students write the SSS congruence argument for ∆AOB ≅ ∆COB step by step, deducing AO = OC and BD ⊥ AC.

Introduce the isosceles trapezium — non-parallel sides equal — and derive Property 2 (base angles equal) by dropping perpendiculars from the ends of the parallel side and using RHS congruence to show the two corner triangles congruent. Students trace the argument in a diagram.

Apply co-interior angle properties to Figure it Out Q3(ii), p.107 ("Find the remaining angles in the trapezium with one marked angle of 105°....") and Figure it Out Q3(iii), p.107 ("Find the remaining angles in the trapezium with one marked angle of 135°...."), then tackle Figure it Out Q5, p.107 ("PAIR and RODS are two rectangles sharing vertex R with OR = 5 cm and ∠P = 30°. Find ∠IOD....") using rectangle angle properties.

Students work on Figure it Out Q9, p.108 ("What type of quadrilateral has opposite sides equal?..."), drawing a diagonal, checking for congruent triangles, and articulating the conclusion as a written justification.

periods.teacher_notes: A common slip in the kite proof is applying SAS instead of SSS — the shared side BD is present in both triangles, so SSS is the correct congruence condition; ask students to list all three pairs of equal sides explicitly before citing the condition. For students who finish quickly, Figure it Out Q5, p.107 offers a rich multi-step reasoning task that weaves together rectangle and angle-sum properties.

periods.activity_title: Classifying Quadrilaterals: Venn Diagrams and True-or-False Proofs

textbook_items_in_class.description: Draw a Venn diagram showing the sets of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles, and squares. Then answer: (i) What quadrilateral is both a kite and a parallelogram? (ii) Can a quadrilateral be both a kite and a rectangle? (iii) Is every kite a rhombus — if not, what is the correct relationship?
True or false: A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square. Justify.
True or false: A quadrilateral having three right angles must be a rectangle. Justify.
True or false: A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other must be a parallelogram. Justify.
True or false: A quadrilateral in which the opposite angles are equal must be a parallelogram. Justify.

time_bands.activity: Students draw the full Venn diagram for Figure it Out Q4, p.107 ("Draw a Venn diagram showing the sets of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles, and squares....") placing each quadrilateral family in its correct region and answering the three sub-questions about intersections, discussing as a class.

Pairs work through Figure it Out Q11(i), p.108 ("True or false: A quadrilateral whose diagonals are equal and bisect each other must be a square....") and Figure it Out Q11(ii), p.108 ("True or false: A quadrilateral having three right angles must be a rectangle...."), producing a written true-or-false verdict with a one-step justification citing the relevant deduction from the chapter.

Class works through Figure it Out Q11(iii), p.108 ("True or false: A quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other must be a parallelogram....") and Figure it Out Q11(v), p.109 ("True or false: A quadrilateral in which the opposite angles are equal must be a parallelogram....") as whole-class discussion, with students proposing counter-examples or proofs.
Short synthesis: students rank the five quadrilateral families from most to fewest properties, explaining one reason for each step in the ranking.

periods.teacher_notes: The Venn diagram is an active reasoning tool here, not decoration — students must use it to answer the sub-questions, so insist the diagram is drawn before the sub-questions are attempted. A rich misconception to surface is the claim that equal and bisecting diagonals make a square (Q11(i) is false: a rectangle has these properties without perpendicular diagonals).

periods.activity_title: Constructing Special Quadrilaterals and Reasoning from Constraints

textbook_items_in_class.description: Construct a square with diagonal 6 cm without using a protractor.

CASE is a square with midpoints U, V, W, X of its sides. Determine what type of quadrilateral UVWX is using geometric reasoning and construction/measurement. Find other ways of inscribing a square within a square with vertices on the sides.
If a quadrilateral has four equal sides and one angle of 90°, will it be a square? Find the answer using geometric reasoning and construction/measurement.
True or false: A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other must be a rhombus. Justify.

time_bands.activity: Students construct the square in Figure it Out Q6, p.107 ("Construct a square with diagonal 6 cm without using a protractor....") using compass and ruler only, relying on the property that a square's diagonals are equal, bisect each other, and are perpendicular. They verify the result by measuring side lengths.

Students work on Figure it Out Q7, p.108 ("CASE is a square with midpoints U, V, W, X of its sides. Determine what type of quadrilateral UVWX is...."), constructing the figure, measuring to conjecture the type, and then writing a reasoning argument using congruent triangles in the corners.

Students investigate Figure it Out Q8, p.108 ("If a quadrilateral has four equal sides and one angle of 90°, will it be a square?...") by construction and deduction, using the rhombus-to-square argument: four equal sides make it a rhombus; one right angle forces all four to be right angles.

Class settles Figure it Out Q11(iv), p.108 ("True or false: A quadrilateral whose diagonals are perpendicular to each other must be a rhombus....") collectively — students propose the kite as a counter-example, discuss, and write a one-sentence verdict with justification.

periods.teacher_notes: The compass-only square construction in Figure it Out Q6, p.107 exploits the perpendicular-bisector property of equal bisecting diagonals proved for squares in Deduction 5; students who have internalised that proof will find the construction natural. Watch for errors in Figure it Out Q7, p.108 where students measure rather than reason — encourage them to identify the congruent triangles at the square's corners before drawing a conclusion.

periods.activity_title: Consolidating Classification: Final True-or-False and Angle-Sum for Non-Convex Shapes

textbook_items_in_class.description: Will the angle sum also be 360° for a non-convex quadrilateral (one with a reflex interior angle)? Find the answer using geometric reasoning and construction/measurement. (Try This)
True or false: A quadrilateral in which all the angles are equal is a rectangle. Justify.
True or false: Isosceles trapeziums are parallelograms. Justify.

time_bands.activity: Students draw a non-convex quadrilateral, measure or compute its interior angles (including the reflex angle), and test Figure it Out Q10, p.108 ("Will the angle sum also be 360° for a non-convex quadrilateral?...") by experiment, then reason using the diagonal-split argument adapted for the non-convex case.

Class works through Figure it Out Q11(vi), p.109 ("True or false: A quadrilateral in which all the angles are equal is a rectangle....") and Figure it Out Q11(vii), p.109 ("True or false: Isosceles trapeziums are parallelograms...."). Students draft individual verdicts with justifications, then a pair-comparison resolves disagreements before a class vote.

Students reflect on which congruence condition (SSS, SAS, AAS, ASA, RHS) appeared in each major deduction of the chapter, building a personal reference table in their notebooks mapping deduction number to congruence condition and quadrilateral property proved.

Closing discussion: teacher poses one open question — 'Which single property, if added to a parallelogram, turns it into a rectangle? A rhombus? A square?' — students answer in writing and share one response each, consolidating the hierarchical classification.

periods.teacher_notes: The non-convex angle-sum question in Figure it Out Q10, p.108 is genuinely surprising — students who expect the answer to be 'no' because reflex angles look different will be challenged to re-examine the diagonal argument; let the discovery unfold rather than pre-answering. The closing congruence-condition table is a retrieval practice tool, not a new topic, and helps students see the chapter's deductive spine as a coherent structure.

goals.section_title: More Quadrilaterals with Parallel Opposite Sides
goals.anchor_description: Using diagonal properties, construct a parallelogram whose diagonals are of lengths 7 cm and 5 cm and intersect at an angle of 140°.
Geoboard Activity: place two rubber bands as perpendicular equal-length diagonals, join the ends to form a quadrilateral, identify and justify its type.

items.prompt: In a rectangle, a diagonal divides the rectangle into two triangles. One of the acute angles formed between the diagonal and a longer side measures 35°. What is the measure of the acute angle formed between the same diagonal and the shorter side?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 55°. The two acute angles the diagonal makes with the sides of the rectangle are complementary because the corner angle of a rectangle is 90°, so 90° − 35° = 55°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the fact that all angles of a rectangle are 90°, so the two acute angles the diagonal makes with the two sides at a corner must sum to 90°.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks the diagonal bisects the corner angle, confusing rectangles with squares.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student doubles 35° rather than subtracting from 90°, misapplying the angle relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the corner angle of the rectangle with the angle between the diagonal and the side.

inclusivity.support: Let the student look back at the 90° corner property of a rectangle and sketch the diagonal with its two angles at the corner.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to generalise: if the diagonal makes angle θ with one side, express the other angle in terms of θ and explain why.

exercise.description: Find all other angles inside the rectangle with one marked angle of 30° (at vertex A).

items.prompt: A kite ABCD has AB = BC and CD = DA. Which of the following correctly describes diagonal BD?

options.label: A
options.text: BD bisects diagonal AC and is perpendicular to AC.

options.label: B
options.text: BD is equal in length to diagonal AC.

options.label: C
options.text: BD bisects the angles at A and C.

options.label: D
options.text: BD and AC bisect each other.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: BD bisects diagonal AC and is perpendicular to AC. By SSS congruence of triangles AOB and COB (where O is the intersection), AO = OC and angle AOB = 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply Property 1 of the kite: the diagonal connecting the vertices between equal-side pairs is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal, derived from SSS congruence.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student conflates kite diagonals with rectangle diagonals, which are equal in length.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student applies the angle-bisecting property to the wrong diagonal — it is BD that bisects angles B and D, not angles A and C.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student attributes the mutual bisection property of parallelograms to the kite, confusing the two families.

inclusivity.support: Let the student re-read the kite definition and draw ABCD, marking the equal sides, before deciding which diagonal is the axis of symmetry.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state one more example of a quadrilateral in which a diagonal is the perpendicular bisector of the other diagonal, and explain why.

exercise.description: Find all the sides and the angles of the quadrilateral obtained by joining two equilateral triangles with sides 4 cm.

items.prompt: A student claims: 'If the diagonals of a quadrilateral are equal and bisect each other, the quadrilateral must be a square.' Is this claim correct? Justify your answer using properties of rectangles and squares established in your textbook.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The claim is false. Equal and mutually bisecting diagonals define a rectangle (Deductions 1–3), but not necessarily a square. A square additionally requires the diagonals to be perpendicular (Deduction 5). A rectangle whose diagonals are not perpendicular is a valid counter-example: it has equal, bisecting diagonals but is not a square.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Distinguish between rectangle (equal + bisecting diagonals) and square (equal + bisecting + perpendicular diagonals) using Deductions 1–3 and Deduction 5.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to write out the five properties of a rectangle and the five properties of a square side by side, then spot the difference.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state the exact extra condition that turns a rectangle into a square and explain which deduction in the chapter proves it.

exercise.description: Can the three equalities (AO = CO, ∠AOB = ∠COD as vertically opposite angles, and AD = CB) be used to establish ∆AOD ≅ ∆COB?

items.prompt: Three angles of a quadrilateral measure 72°, 115°, and 98°. A student says the fourth angle must be 75°. Verify whether the student is correct and explain the reasoning using the angle-sum property of a quadrilateral.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The fourth angle is 360° − (72° + 115° + 98°) = 360° − 285° = 75°. The student is correct. The angle sum of any quadrilateral is 360°, derived by splitting it with one diagonal into two triangles each summing to 180°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the quadrilateral angle-sum theorem (360°) by subtracting the sum of the three known angles from 360°.

inclusivity.support: Let the student recall that a diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles and add 180° + 180° before proceeding.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to explain what happens to the angle-sum argument if the quadrilateral is non-convex, linking to the extension question in the textbook.

exercise.description: Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 40° (at vertex R).

items.section_title: More Quadrilaterals with Parallel Opposite Sides
items.prompt: In parallelogram PQRS, ∠P = 3x + 10° and ∠Q = 5x − 30°. Using the properties of a parallelogram established in your textbook, find the value of x and all four angles. Justify each step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary (Deduction 6), so (3x + 10) + (5x − 30) = 180. This gives 8x − 20 = 180, so 8x = 200, x = 25. Then ∠P = 3(25) + 10 = 85°, ∠Q = 5(25) − 30 = 95°. Opposite angles are equal, so ∠R = ∠P = 85° and ∠S = ∠Q = 95°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use Deduction 6: adjacent angles of a parallelogram sum to 180° (co-interior angles on parallel lines) to set up the equation, then apply the equal-opposite-angles property.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to first state which pair of angles in a parallelogram are supplementary, using the co-interior angle idea from parallel lines.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to identify what additional property would make PQRS a rectangle, and compute what x would need to be.

exercise.description: Find the remaining angles in the parallelogram with one marked angle of 110° (at vertex E).

items.prompt: Prove that in any rhombus, the two diagonals intersect at right angles. State clearly which congruence condition you use and why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Let the diagonals of rhombus ABCD meet at O. In triangles AOB and COB: AO = CO (diagonals of a rhombus bisect each other, from the parallelogram property), AB = CB (all sides of a rhombus are equal), and OB is common. By SSS congruence, ∆AOB ≅ ∆COB. Therefore ∠AOB = ∠COB. But ∠AOB + ∠COB = 180° (angles on a straight line), so each equals 90°. Hence the diagonals are perpendicular.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use SSS congruence on the two triangles at the diagonal intersection, then deduce that two equal supplementary angles must each be 90° (Deduction 10).

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to first list which sides and segments are equal at the intersection point before naming a congruence condition.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to identify which other quadrilateral family also has perpendicular diagonals and explain whether the proof method would be identical or different.

exercise.description: Using diagonal properties, construct a rhombus whose diagonals are of lengths 4 cm and 5 cm.

items.prompt: In an isosceles trapezium PQRS with PQ ∥ SR, the non-parallel sides PS and QR are equal. A student claims that ∠P = ∠Q. Justify this claim using the properties of an isosceles trapezium from your textbook.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Drop perpendiculars from S and R to PQ, meeting PQ at points S′ and R′ respectively. The two right-angled triangles PS S′ and QR R′ have PS = QR (given), SS′ = RR′ (perpendicular distance between parallels is constant), and both have a right angle. By RHS congruence, ∆PS S′ ≅ ∆QR R′. Therefore PS′ = QR′, giving ∠P = ∠Q.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Drop perpendiculars to the parallel side and apply RHS congruence to the two corner right-angled triangles (Property 2 of the isosceles trapezium).

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to draw the perpendiculars first and label all equal parts before attempting the congruence argument.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to determine whether the other pair of base angles (∠S and ∠R) are also equal and provide a one-sentence justification.

exercise.description: Find the remaining angles in the trapezium with one marked angle of 105°.

items.prompt: A student draws a Venn diagram and places the rhombus inside the set of kites, arguing that every rhombus is a kite. Is this correct? Justify your answer by comparing the definitions of a kite and a rhombus.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: A kite is defined as a quadrilateral with two pairs of consecutive equal sides. In a rhombus, all four sides are equal, so any two consecutive sides are equal — meaning a rhombus satisfies the kite definition. However, not every kite is a rhombus (a kite with unequal pairs of consecutive sides is not a rhombus). Therefore a rhombus is a special case of a kite, and in the Venn diagram the rhombus set should be inside (or intersect) the kite set, not the other way around.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the definitions: a rhombus has all sides equal, satisfying the kite's consecutive-equal-sides condition, so every rhombus is a kite but not vice versa.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to write the definition of a kite and the definition of a rhombus side by side, then check whether the rhombus definition satisfies the kite definition.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask what additional property a kite would need to become a rhombus, and draw the corrected Venn diagram showing the relationship.

exercise.description: Draw a Venn diagram showing the sets of parallelograms, kites, rhombuses, rectangles, and squares.

items.prompt: Can a quadrilateral have four equal sides and not be a square? Justify your answer using properties of rhombuses and rectangles from your textbook.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. A rhombus has four equal sides but its angles need not all be 90°. The angle-sum theorem gives 360° for four angles, and adjacent angles of a rhombus are supplementary; if any one angle differs from 90°, the adjacent angle also differs from 90°, giving a non-square rhombus. A square is the special rhombus in which all angles are 90°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Cite the rhombus definition (four equal sides, adjacent angles supplementary) and the additional condition (all angles 90°) that distinguishes a square from a general rhombus.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to sketch a rhombus that is clearly not a square (a very flat one) and list its side and angle properties.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state what single additional property on the angles, or on the diagonals, is both necessary and sufficient to turn a rhombus into a square.

exercise.description: Construct a square with diagonal 6 cm without using a protractor.

items.prompt: A non-convex quadrilateral is drawn with one interior reflex angle. A classmate claims that the angle-sum of 360° no longer holds for such a quadrilateral. Using the diagonal-splitting argument from your textbook, explain whether the classmate is correct.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The classmate is incorrect. Drawing a diagonal from a non-reflex vertex of the non-convex quadrilateral still splits it into two triangles, each with angle sum 180°, giving a total of 360°. The six triangle angles still pair up exactly into the four interior angles of the quadrilateral (one of which is reflex), so the sum remains 360°.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the diagonal-splitting argument: the diagonal creates two triangles regardless of convexity, so the total angle sum remains 180° + 180° = 360°.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to draw a non-convex quadrilateral, label the reflex angle, and draw the diagonal, then count the six triangle angles.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to consider whether the diagonal can always be drawn from any vertex of a non-convex quadrilateral, and what happens if the chosen vertex is the reflex one.

exercise.description: Will the angle sum also be 360° for a non-convex quadrilateral (one with a reflex interior angle)?

items.section_title: More Quadrilaterals with Parallel Opposite Sides
items.prompt: A parallelogram ABCD has diagonals AC = 10 cm and BD = 6 cm that bisect each other. The diagonals intersect at point O at an angle of 50°. Find the length of OA, OC, OB, and OD. Then state the angles of the four triangles formed at O.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Since the diagonals bisect each other (Deduction 8), OA = OC = 10/2 = 5 cm and OB = OD = 6/2 = 3 cm. At O, the diagonals cross at 50°, so the four angles are 50°, 130°, 50°, 130° (vertically opposite angles are equal and adjacent angles are supplementary on a straight line). The four triangles at O have angles: two triangles with angles 50°, and two with angles 130° at O, with the remaining angles in each triangle summing to the supplement.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the diagonal-bisection property of parallelograms (Deduction 8) to find the four half-lengths, then use vertically opposite and supplementary angle properties at the intersection.

inclusivity.support: Draw the parallelogram with its diagonals and label O, then use the bisection property to halve each diagonal before dealing with the angles.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the crossing angle to a variable θ and express all four intersection angles in terms of θ, then identify for what value of θ the parallelogram becomes a rhombus.

exercise.description: Using diagonal properties, construct a parallelogram whose diagonals are of lengths 7 cm and 5 cm and intersect at an angle of 140°.

items.prompt: Two isosceles triangle cutouts, each with sides 10 cm, 10 cm, and 8 cm, are joined along their 8 cm base. What quadrilateral is formed? Find all four side lengths and all four angles of the resulting quadrilateral. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Joining two congruent isosceles triangles along their common base (8 cm) produces a rhombus. All four sides of the rhombus equal the equal sides of the triangles = 10 cm. To find the angles: in each isosceles triangle, the two base angles are equal. Using the cosine rule or the fact that the triangle has sides 10, 10, 8: the base angle α satisfies cos α = (10² + 10² − 8²)/(2·10·10) = (200 − 64)/200 = 136/200 = 0.68, so α ≈ 47.16° (accept ≈ 47°). The apex angle of each triangle = 180° − 2(47°) = 86°. The two angles of the rhombus at the joining edge each equal 2 × 47° = 94°, and the two angles at the apex each equal 86°. Check: 94° + 86° + 94° + 86° = 360°. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Identify the rhombus by the equal-sides argument from the triangle-joining activity, then compute angles by applying base-angle equality in the isosceles triangles and the supplementary-adjacent-angles property of a rhombus.

inclusivity.support: Prompt the student to first check whether all four sides of the resulting quadrilateral are equal, then use the triangle's base angles to find the rhombus angles.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify the result using the rhombus property that adjacent angles are supplementary, and confirm the sum is 360°.
